title: Praise and blame
hook: favor and disgrace both unsettle us; care for the world as for your own body (Tao Te Ching 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, five colors: too much to see, and the eye goes numb. Your line was less to see. What did you turn down, and what came back? Day one thousand seventy-five.

A cook in a busy kitchen gets two messages from the dining room in the same minute. Table four sends compliments to the chef. Table nine sends a plate back. One sounds like sun, the other like a cold draft. Follow the cook through the next hour. Both messages are still replaying while the next orders wait. Both pull attention off the stove. Both have quietly handed the steering wheel to someone in the dining room. Chapter thirteen of the Tao Te Ching puts praise and blame side by side and says something that sounds odd at first: they're the same kind of trouble.
screen: `TWO MESSAGES FROM THE DINING ROOM.` → `COMPLIMENTS, AND A PLATE SENT BACK.` → `THE SAME KIND OF TROUBLE.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. The chapter opens by saying that favor and disgrace both startle a person. Not just disgrace. Favor too. It explains why: when you get favor, you're startled; when you lose it, you're startled again. Praise isn't a resting place. It's a thing you can now lose. Second, a hint about why favor is unsettling. The chapter calls favor the lower thing. Readers take this in more than one way. Some hear it as: to be favored is to stand beneath whoever does the favoring. Their approval becomes something you need. Others hear simply that favor is worth less than people think. Either way, praise ties you to someone else's opinion as surely as blame does. Third, the body. The chapter then asks a startling question: why do we have great troubles? Because we have a body, a self. If there were no self, what trouble could reach us? Some readers hear this not as a call to give up the body, but as pointing at the part of us that keeps score of how we're seen, where so much distress gathers. Fourth, the turn outward. The chapter ends by saying that a person who values the whole world the way they value their own body can be trusted with the world. The care you'd spend guarding your reputation, spend on everything else instead. That's the move: from how am I seen, to what needs care. Praise and blame stop being the steering wheel, and the work, and the people, come back into view.
screen: `FAVOR AND DISGRACE BOTH STARTLE.` · `FAVOR IS THE LOWER THING.` · `TROUBLE GATHERS AROUND THE SELF.` · `CARE FOR THE WORLD AS FOR YOUR BODY.` · then, large: `FAVOR AND DISGRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one praise pass by. Settle, and bring to mind a recent compliment, large or small. Notice where it lands in the body: a warmth, a lift, maybe a small wish to hear it again. Don't push it away, and don't hold on to it. Let it be like a car passing on the street outside: here, then gone. If a criticism shows up instead, treat it the same way. Then let your attention turn outward, to one person or one task that needs care today. The bell holds the time.
Praise and blame. In chapter thirteen, favor and disgrace: two sides of one worry, both of them tied to someone else's opinion. Today's word.
Your line: favor and disgrace. When praise or criticism lands today, say the line to yourself, let it pass like a car outside, and go back to what needs care. Day one thousand seventy-five.

howItsDone: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching use chapter thirteen as a check after praise or criticism: they notice how both pull at them, and turn their attention back to the work or the people in front of them.

fork.setup: your boss praises your work in front of everyone. by chapter thirteen's light, what's the trouble with that?
options: none: praise is pure good news.
now there's something to lose, and it startles you both ways.

fork.reveal: favor startles when you get it and again when you lose it. the chapter doesn't say refuse it; it says notice the hook.

original.note: Chinese: favor and disgrace, the pair chapter thirteen opens with.

trapdoor: what you thought: praise good, blame bad.
what it means: both hand the steering wheel to someone else's opinion; getting favor startles, and so does losing it.
what a scholar hears: the chapter calls favor the lower thing, read either as being beneath the one who favors you or as favor being worth less than it seems.

notes: Chapter 13 paraphrased throughout (Legge 1891 not quoted: his rendering opens 'Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared', which the writer could not confirm word for word).

'Favor is the lower thing' (寵為下) is read differently by translators; two readings are given without ranking. Some editions read the line differently (e.g. 'favor is above, disgrace below'); a scholar should check which reading to present.
'Because we have a self to protect' paraphrases 吾所以有大患者，為吾有身 ('because I have a body'); the move from 'body' to 'a self to protect' is interpretive. Confirm it is fair.
The closing lines (one who values the world as his own body can be entrusted with it) are paraphrased; confirm.

Editor pass: hook rewritten from phone notifications to a kitchen scene, because day 1074's hook was a phone screen; the hook no longer tells the listener what plays in their head; 'a self to protect' brought closer to the text ('a body, a self'), with the score-keeping reading attributed to some readers (teach, match and myth).
